title: Sayak Paul (@RisingSayak)
clean_title: Tools for library maintenance using agents, including Serge for PR review
summary:
Wanted to list some tools that we have built with agents to make library maintenance more fun and less burdensome.
The first one is obvious -- an agentic PR reviewer, aka "Serge".
It respects the lib-specific rules, lets you choose between different models, and lets you edit the synthetic review before posting.
The rationale here is that the lib maintainers already bring years of experience in reviewing, and if that can be precisely written as "rules", it can help an agent drive a good-first review pass, often helping contributors get rid of pesky stuff.
But an actual human being will also have to review the PR before merging. That is a rule we don't take lightly.
Check it out here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLFpEAFagAANMcJ.jpg
clean_summary: Sayak Paul shares tools built with agents to make library maintenance more enjoyable and less burdensome. The first tool is Serge, an agentic pull request reviewer that respects library-specific rules, allows model selection, and enables editing of the synthetic review before posting. The idea is that experienced human reviewers can encode their rules to help the agent generate a good first review pass, assisting contributors in removing common issues. Human review remains essential before merging. Check it out here.

clean_title: Best-of-N as a strong baseline for diffusion test-time scaling
summary:
We show that best-of-N (BoN) is a much better baseline for diffusion test-time scaling when done right.
Our core premise is that NFEs provide a false sense of efficiency by ignoring several underlying factors, such as verifier costs.
We then introduce Flash-BoN, which encourages broader exploration of samples than repeated intermediate validation.
Overall, our findings are simple:
1. Report NFEs AND wallclock time (so that the algorithms that verify more frequently are validated appropriately)
2. Spend (test-time) compute on exploring more rather than frequent intermediate validations
When we combined the two, we see that BoN either outperforms or is on par with other fancier techniques.
Extended thread 👇
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2076703831602397184/img/xtjZSFv_q_iO5ZuK.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2076703831602397184/vid/avc1/480x270/0ZmOlRiEZGT2W7EY.mp4?tag=14

The main findings are that NFEs and wallclock time should both be reported, and test-time compute should focus on exploring more rather than validating often. clean_title: Transformers models now run in vLLM at native speed, matching or beating hand-written implementations
summary:
Big unlock for open-source AI inference: Hugging Face Transformers models can now run in vLLM at native speed, often matching or beating hand-written implementations.
Until now, every new architecture often needed to be built twice:
- Once in Transformers for training and research
- Again in vLLM for fast production inference
That duplication slowed down new models, added maintenance, and created room for implementations to diverge. Now, model authors can implement an architecture once in Transformers and immediately benefit from vLLM’s optimized inference stack.
In our benchmarks, the Transformers backend matched or beat native vLLM throughput across models from 4B to 235B parameters, including tensor parallel and MoE setups. One readable model implementation can now power training, fine-tuning, evaluation, RL rollouts, and production inference.
The conventional wisdom is that abstractions make systems slower. The best abstractions make the whole ecosystem faster.
Write the model once. Deploy it everywhere.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNIk1Z9WsAACvuN.jpg

summary:
The experience of having worked on a bunch of technical things hands-on in the pre-agents era is largely a blessing to me!
Sure, most of the time agents are implementing complex (by my standards) stuff almost one-shot (and that's very productive!). But it's those ~5% of workflows where your hard-earned experience is genuinely the deal-breaker.
Even in the pre-agents era, it's almost exactly those workflows where you'd catch a sweat. I don't think the system design part of it has changed much at all, at least not for the complex stuff.
I don't think people without this experience will ever be able to fathom what I am talking about.

But from there on, he undertook a rigorous effort to ensure the community becomes comfortable generating and reading profile traces in PyTorch.
Almost all the serious practitioners I know of who are working in this space know that profiling is an absolute basic if one wants to understand WTF is going on inside an accelerator. Why is it idle? Why is the model not fast enough? What can be optimized further?
However, the chatter around profiling seemed quite quiet, almost as if everyone knew it fully. I think we can agree that it's not the case at all.
Hopefully, the three-part blog series takes a good first step at TEACHING you the importance of profiling and how to use it in the grand scheme of things.

title: Sayak Paul (@RisingSayak)
summary:
This was our first incident of this kind, and we want to thank OpenAI for its transparency about what happened and for the collaboration.
Fortunately, Hugging Face is used to being a target of (human) hackers: we sit at the centre of the AI ecosystem, with all the models, datasets, evaluations, and libraries. Over the years, our security team has built formidable expertise and uses top open-source models to process information and respond quickly.
But this incident also reinforced my belief in the importance of access to capable open-weight models for cyber defence. When a frontier model is attacking you and moving laterally inside your infrastructure, defenders need wide access to near-frontier tools within hours or even minutes, rather than being pointed towards a closed-door, vetted application programme for model access.
Transparency and access to capable AI systems are as important for responding to threats as they are for democratization and innovation. We believe open-science and open-source AI are among the strongest tools for building a safer, more collaborative and more secure AI ecosystem.
Quoting @sama
we had a significant security incident during evaluation of our models. we are sharing what we have learned so far. thanks to @huggingface for the partnership on this.
